title: What can we say about the HCF of five kinds of pairs?
description: Five kinds of pairs are tried with examples: even numbers next to each other, odd numbers next to each other, any two even numbers, numbers next to each other, and co-prime numbers. The gap between the numbers explains each statement. The answer is checked with fresh pairs.
teaching_notes: One idea: a common factor of two numbers also goes into the gap between them, and that fact explains each statement about the highest common factor. Ask the class to test each statement with a pair of their own before the working is shown. Watch for students who say two for odd numbers that are two apart.

video_script.why: The child found the highest common factor of pairs next to each other and now makes general statements for five kinds of pairs, with reasons.
video_script.substitution: Try a few pairs of each kind, then use the gap between the numbers and the evenness of the numbers to say why the statement holds.
video_script.anchor: Five kinds of pairs in a column: even numbers next to each other; odd numbers next to each other; two even numbers; numbers next to each other; co-prime numbers.
video_script.payoff_line: The answers are two, one, an even number, one and one

final_answer.spoken: two, one, an even number, one and one

never_show: a kind's answer before its own step
maths_rules: (a) 4 and 6, 10 and 12: both even and 2 apart, a common factor goes into 2, so the HCF is 2
(b) 5 and 7, 11 and 13: 2 apart but odd, so 2 is not a common factor and the HCF is 1
(c) 6 and 10 give 2, 8 and 12 give 4: 2 divides both, so the HCF is even, at least 2
(d) 7 and 8, 20 and 21: 1 apart, so the HCF is 1
(e) co-prime numbers have HCF 1 by meaning
check: 12 and 18 have HCF 6, which is even; 20 and 21 have HCF 1
video_script.design: One idea: a common factor goes into the gap between the numbers. The five kinds stay in the anchor band all video and each step lights the kinds it uses. The check tries a fresh pair for the third kind and the fourth kind.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must make a general statement about the highest common factor of five kinds of pairs.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Even numbers next to each other. Odd numbers next to each other. Any two even numbers.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Then numbers next to each other.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Last, co-prime numbers, which means numbers whose highest common factor is one.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>What can we say about each kind?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, the first kind. Take four and six, and ten and twelve. Each pair is two apart.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Both numbers are even, so two goes in, and the highest common factor is two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second kind is five and seven, and eleven and thirteen. These are also two apart, but they are odd, so two does not go in.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The highest common factor is one.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the third kind. Take six and ten, and eight and twelve. Their highest common factors are two and four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two goes into every even number, so it is always a common factor.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The highest common factor is even, and at least two.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>The highest common factor is one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Co-prime numbers have no common factor other than one, so their highest common factor is one.
